text:
Stocks' shock absorber could be masking a much uglier downside.

Peter Tchir says popular income funds may be propping up stocks, but outflows could trigger a rapid downturn

"One problem I think the stock market has that Bitcoin doesn't have is all the vol suppression strategies tied to it."

"Everywhere you look, there's income oriented funds that are selling vol in the S&P 500, selling it on Nasdaq 100, selling it on individual stocks."

"I suspect it's part of why the buy the dip has been so successful. I would watch, like, the JEPIs and JEPQs of the world to see if they get any outflows."

"I suspect, though, if it breaks, it gets really ugly very quickly. And you would get a very rapid downturn as those sorts of strategies unwind."

"All these vol suppression strategies are much bigger and much more prevalent than they were 5, 10 years ago."

text:
Yikes. Anthropic just pulled the exact accounting trick that companies did in 2000 bubble for IPO.

They hid all their expenses via convertible notes redeemable at IPO. $108 billion worth.

Dotcom firms often paid suppliers, ad agencies, lawyers and even landlords with stock or equity to save cash. AOL swapped shares for services and ads (e.g., Homestore, DrKoop). Telecom suppliers like Lucent, Cisco and Nortel used vendor financing, sometimes with equity or warrants, to drive equipment sales.

BREAKING: Verizon CEO admits he assumes everything SpaceX says it will do, it will do, and execute flawlessly, and says he takes its terrestrial moves "quite seriously"

Dan Schulman (CEO): “I also operate under the assumption that everything SpaceX says they will do, they will do, and that they will execute flawlessly. That’s my operating assumption on it. I think to assume anything else, makes no sense from my perspective."

"And everything that we’ve seen so far, all of their announcements, everything we’re hearing in the market, and I’ll talk about that in just a second, is so far the path that we’ve basically predicted that they would do."

"We always knew that they needed a terrestrial network to have any chance at providing a competitive service. I don’t really need to re-review the satellite beam physics, but just suffice to say that without a terrestrial network, their addressable market for broadband services is relatively small.”

"It’s in very rural areas, and their service just can’t compete with a terrestrial network. In suburban and urban areas where like 98% of our revenues are, we’re somewhere between 100 to 1,000 times more efficient than they are. And when you think about wireless, it’s even more difficult with them to compete on a satellite basis."

"And so I think that SpaceX realizes this, and they’re exploring a potential path to creating a terrestrial network. It’s not surprising they said it on their call, so I think we should take it quite seriously.

We know exactly what they're going to do. We know who they're talking to on towers. There's no magic wand. There's no secret sauce. There's no shortcut.

They're going to look at 65,000–80,000 macro sites. They're going to need backhaul, RAN, and a tremendous amount of spectrum. It's going to take a minimum of four to six years to fully build that out. It's going to cost hundreds and hundreds of billions of dollars, I assume somewhere between $300 billion and $500 billion.

Then they need to build retail, customer service, back office systems, et cetera. All of that gets them basically the same network and same capabilities and same cost structure as what we have today. Then sometime over the next four to six years, they have the possibility of becoming the sixth, not the fourth, the sixth competitor in the market.

You can be sure over these next three to five years or six years, we are not going to be standing still.
